task.openingSentence:
Hey Hey is a project and product management tool. A project's knowledge is a tree of features, each one a product capability that says what users get rather than how it is built. Each feature has requirements: separate statements of one thing it must do. Tasks are the units of work that implement them. An AI agent is about to work on the task below and should be shown the requirements that bear on it, because reading requirements that do not matter costs time and distracts.

Work can be implementation, or it can be research that studies, compares or reports on other work; for research, the work it studies is the subject. This is that task, described by state.task.description with its acceptance criteria in state.task.acceptance_criteria. It works on a parent feature, described by state.parent_feature.description. The requirements of the parent feature are the candidates, listed under state.requirements. They are grouped but stored and judged separately, and each defines one aspect of the feature, so judge each narrowly and concretely.
task.relevanceQuestion:
Does {candidate} apply to the {focal}? It applies when the task delivers or changes the behavior the requirement states, could break it, or has it as a key part of what the task works on. Sharing a feature is not enough: a task usually touches a few of a feature's requirements and none of the others.

Examples, for a task called Stop reminders once an invoice is paid, under a parent feature called Overdue Invoice Reminders:
- "Reminders stop once the invoice is paid." Applies: the task delivers this.
- "A reminder email is sent when an invoice is 30 days past its due date." Applies: the change sits in the sending of reminders and must not stop them for unpaid invoices.
- "Customers can unsubscribe from reminders." Does not apply: the task neither changes nor can break unsubscribing.
- "Finance admins can see which reminders were sent." Does not apply: the task does not change that list.

criteria.implements: The {focal} implements or directly changes the behavior the {candidate} describes
criteria.informs: The {focal} does not implement the {candidate} but the {candidate} is a key part of what {focal} will work on
criteria.same_feature_unrelated: The {candidate} is about behavior the {focal} neither changes nor can break
criteria.other: The {candidate} is about a different feature or behavior

task.openingSentence:
Hey Hey is a project and product management tool. A project's knowledge is a tree of features, each one a product capability that says what users get rather than how it is built, with tasks beneath them that implement the work. An AI agent is about to carry out one task and can read only a few connected entities in full. The goal is to pick the ones worth reading, because reading one that does not matter costs time and distracts the agent.

Work can be implementation, or it can be research that studies, compares or reports on other work; for research, the work it studies is the subject. This is that task, described by state.task.description with its acceptance criteria in state.task.acceptance_criteria. {parent} Broader features sit above it (its ancestors, state.ancestors). The other branches under those broader features sit beside it (state.ancestor_siblings and state.siblings). Narrower features sit below it (state.children), and other entities are connected by links (state.edges and state.mentions). A broader feature describes a whole area of the product in general terms, so most of what it says is not specific to this work. A neighbouring branch usually covers a different capability. Being nearby in the tree is not a reason to read something.
task.relevanceQuestion:
Would someone carrying out the {focal} need to read {candidate} to get the work right? Judge by what it says, not by where it sits in the tree. It is needed when it states a rule, interface or constraint the change has to follow or could break, describes behavior the task delivers or changes, or is part of what the task works on. It is not needed when it only names the wider area, covers a different capability, or would read the same whether or not the task was done.

Examples, for a task called Stop reminders once an invoice is paid, under a parent feature called Overdue Invoice Reminders:
- A broader feature, Billing, says "An invoice counts as paid at the moment a payment covers its full amount." Needed: the task has to stop reminders at exactly that moment.
- A broader feature, Customer Accounts, says "Each business has an account that holds its customers and users." Not needed: it describes the wider area and states nothing the task must follow.
- A feature on another branch, Account Settings, says "People can change their name, email and password." Not needed: a different capability.
- A narrower feature, Reminder Scheduling, says "Every day, each invoice that is still unpaid is queued for a reminder." Needed: this is the behavior the task changes.

criteria.implements: The {focal} delivers or changes the behavior the {candidate} describes
criteria.informs: The {focal} does not deliver the {candidate}, but the {candidate} states a rule, interface or constraint that the {focal} relies on or must stay consistent with
criteria.same_feature_unrelated: The {candidate} is related to the {focal} only by where it sits in the project or by a link, such as a broader area the {focal} belongs to or a neighbour covering a different capability. The {focal} changes, relies on and breaks nothing the {candidate} describes
criteria.other: The {candidate} is about a different feature or behavior

Judging only by the line shown for {candidate}, how is it connected to the user's request about the {focal}? Each line starts with how it is connected, then the title and kind, then the reason for the link or the requirement that cites it when there is one. A citation by a requirement is strong evidence of a real connection. A shared name or broad topic alone is not. A link can be real and still not matter: judge whether the user's request touches or changes what the candidate provides, not whether the focal work has some dependency on it.

Examples, for work on Checkout when the user asks to handle failed payments and retries:

- DEPENDS_ON outbound · Order State (feature) · Retries rely on telling unpaid orders from orders whose payment is awaiting confirmation. supplies: the work relies on what it provides.
- RELATED_TO inbound · Double charge on payment timeout (bug) · A timeout can leave a customer charged twice. reports_problem: the retry work has to handle it.
- mentioned in Checkout · Payment Provider Notes (design_doc). possibly_connected: the line gives no reason, but a payment document could bear on retries.
- fulfills requirement · Receipt Typography (task) · "Receipts use the brand font and spacing" of Checkout. unrelated: it only controls fonts and spacing.
- DEPENDS_ON outbound · Order State (feature) · Checkout relies on Order State to tell paid orders from unpaid ones. unrelated: a real dependency, but the request about retries does not touch it.
- sibling-via-parent · Gift Card Redemption (feature). unrelated: nothing but its place in the tree connects it to the request.
- sibling-via-parent · Retry modal.  supplies: the work relies on what it provides.
- sibling-via-parent · (Spike) incremental backoff algorithms.  governs: it decided the algorithm the retry should use

openingSentence.task:
Hey Hey is a project and product management tool. A project's knowledge is a tree of features, each one a product capability that says what users get rather than how it is built. Features have requirements; tasks implement the work, design documents explain intended behavior, and contracts state promises that other work relies on. An AI agent is addressing a user's request and has read the items under state.entities in full. It will drop the ones that do not apply. Missing an item that mattered is worse than reading one that did not, so an item is dropped only when it clearly does not bear on the work or the ask.

Work can be implementation, or it can be research that studies, compares or reports on other work; for research, the work it studies is the subject. This is that task, described by state.task.description with its acceptance criteria in state.task.acceptance_criteria. {parent} The user's ask is in state.ask.text. Each item under state.entities is the full text of one feature, task, design document, contract or other work item, starting with its title. An item applies when it bears on the task or on the ask; it does not need to bear on both.

read_check.question:
Does {candidate} apply to the {focal} or the user's ask? It applies when it states a rule, interface or constraint the work must follow or could break, describes behavior the work delivers or changes, records a decision or known problem the work has to account for, is named in the work's own text, or is work that the work studies, compares with, reports on or follows on from. It does not apply when it describes a capability the work neither names, studies, changes nor relies on, and would read the same whether or not the work was done.

Examples, for a task called Stop reminders once an invoice is paid, with the ask "reminders keep going out after customers pay":
- A design document, Reminder Scheduling, says "Every day, each invoice that is still unpaid is queued for a reminder." Applies: this is the behavior the task changes.
- A task, Let people change their notification email, says "People can set the address their reminders go to." Does not apply: it is about reminders, but the task neither changes nor relies on where they are sent.

Examples, for a research task called Find out why reminder emails arrive late, with the ask "are reminders queued or sent straight away?":
- A task, Queue reminders in batches overnight, says "Reminders are collected during the day and sent in one batch at 02:00." Applies: the research studies how reminders are sent, and this task is the behavior it has to explain.
- A feature, Invoice PDF layout, says "Invoices are rendered with the customer's logo in the header." Does not apply: it is about invoices but says nothing about when reminders are sent.

criteria.applies: The {candidate} states something the {focal} delivers, changes, relies on, studies, names in its own text or could break, given the user's ask
criteria.does_not_apply: The {candidate} describes a capability the {focal} neither names, studies, changes nor relies on, and would read the same whether or not the work was done

task.openingSentence: Hey Hey is a project and product management tool. A project's knowledge is a tree of features, each one a product capability; tasks implement the work. A Decision is a choice the project has deliberately made, with its rationale and consequences. Work that would go against an applicable Decision must be raised with the user before it is done, so an agent starting work reads the Decisions that apply to it. The work is a task, described by state.task.description with its acceptance criteria in state.task.acceptance_criteria. {parent} The user's request is in state.ask.text; it says what the agent is about to do, so judge the Decision against the request first and the task as its setting. A Decision applies when the request would make, change or have to respect the choice it records, even when the Decision sits under a different feature. It does not apply merely because it is about the same feature, or because it is about the product in general.
task.relevanceQuestion: How much does {candidate} apply to what the user asked of the {focal}?

criteria.implements: Doing what the request asks would make, change or go against the choice the {candidate} records. Example: a request to store each direct user edit in a new table, against a Decision that product data lives in the core entity types.
criteria.informs: The request does not change the choice, but carrying it out must respect the {candidate}: its consequences constrain how the work is done. Example: a request to let users save edits that are approved automatically, against a Decision that every content change is recorded as a proposal.
criteria.same_feature_unrelated: The {candidate} is about the same feature or area as the {focal}, but nothing the request asks touches the choice it records. Example: a request to add a per-address limit on demo sandboxes, against a Decision about how new users are admitted to the beta.
criteria.other: The {candidate} is about a different part of the product, and the request neither makes nor must respect its choice. Example: a request to shorten onboarding questions, against a Decision about the source-code licence.
